projects.title: Approval cutoff for a consumer lender
projects.result: +$7.1M realized NPV from a new approval cutoff, at the same bad rate
projects.what: realized NPV from a new approval cutoff, at the same bad rate
projects.question: Can a new approval cutoff increase approvals at the same bad rate?
projects.answer: Yes. A scorecard cutoff approves more applicants at the same bad rate and adds $7.1M of realized NPV on the 2015 loans.

keyline.h: It approves more applicants with no more defaults
keyline.p: Approval rate: 85.7% vs. 84.5% today. Bad rate (default rate of approved loans): 12.5%, held equal.

keyline.h: The gain holds under every cost assumption tested
keyline.p: Realized NPV against the current policy: +$7.1M. Lowest result in the stress test: +$5.1M.

keyline.h: A small test limits the risk of the change
keyline.p: Start on 10% of applications. Stop if 12-month defaults rise 1 point.

problem.scene: A consumer lender offers unsecured 36-month loans. A risk grade puts each applicant in a sub-grade from A1 to G5. The lender approves the best sub-grades and declines the others.
problem.now: The business wants more approvals, but Risk does not accept a higher bad rate. The loans from 2015 lost $32.9M.
problem.want: More approvals at the same bad rate of 12.5%, and more realized NPV from the same applicants.

scqa: A consumer lender approves applicants by credit grade. Loans from 2013–2014: realized NPV +$71.7M.
What changed, and what it cost
In 2015, interest rates fell and default rates rose in every grade. Loans from 2015: realized NPV –$32.9M.
Q: How can the lender approve more customers with no increase in losses?
Replace the credit grade with a risk scorecard. Approval rate 84.5% → 85.7% at a bad rate of 12.5%. Realized NPV +$7.1M. Next step: a test on 10% of applications.
projects.tree_q: Is the new cutoff good enough to test on real applications?
tree: Does the scorecard approve more applicants at the same bad rate?
Approval rate 85.7% vs. 84.5%, bad rate 12.5% for both.
Do the swapped applicants make money?
The applicants that the scorecard approves in place of others add $8.3M of realized NPV.
Does the gain hold when the cost assumptions change?
At least +$5.1M under every cost assumption tested.
Is a more complex model worth it?
A gradient boosting model ranks risk only 1.5 KS points better, below the 2-point rule set before the test. The scorecard stays, and it gives a reason for each decline.
Does the cutoff alone fix the loss on the 2015 loans?
The cutoff recovers $7.1M of a $32.9M loss. A pricing test for grades A to C must go with it.

method.h: Both policies run on the same 2015 applicants, and every number is an actual outcome
steps: Define the current policy on booked loans
The current policy approves the best sub-grades, up to about 85% of the 2015 applicants.
Use the declined group as the check group
The lender booked loans in the lowest sub-grades too. Each of these loans has a real outcome: default or no default, and the cash it returned.
Compare the two policies on actual outcomes
The scorecard approves the same number of applicants in a different order. The comparison uses the actual default rate and the realized NPV of the applicants that change sides.
notes: The scorecard learns from the loans of 2013–2014 and is tested on the loans of 2015, which it never saw.
Grade, sub-grade and interest rate are not inputs to the scorecard, because they are results of the lender's own policy.

The current policy is my assumption. The public data shows only booked loans, not the lender's approval rule. The result shows a method and the likely size of the gain. The test on 10% of applications measures the gain against the real policy.

steps: Get the data
Which data shows the actual outcome of each applicant?
Clean and prepare
Which loans, which target and which columns are allowed? What did the current policy return?
Split the data
How do we test the model on a period that it never saw?
Build the score
Which columns and which model type rank applicants by risk best?
Calibrate and explain
Is the probability of default at the right level, and is there a reason for each decline?
Compare the policies
Is the new policy better than the current one, in model metrics and in dollars?
Set the cutoff and the test
Where does the cutoff go, and how do we test it with real applicants?

projects.title: Transaction policy for card fraud
projects.result: $64k lower monthly cost of fraud, false declines and reviews
projects.what: lower total cost of fraud, false declines and reviews
projects.question: Which policy gives the lowest total cost of fraud, false declines and reviews?
projects.answer: A three-tier policy (approve, review, decline) on a fraud score cuts the total monthly cost by $64k and keeps false declines under the 3% cap.

keyline.h: It stops almost twice the fraud dollars
keyline.p: Share of fraud dollars stopped: 71.2% vs. 38.4% for a fixed rule set.

keyline.h: The total cost falls, not only the fraud loss
keyline.p: Total monthly cost = fraud loss that gets through + cost of false declines + cost of reviews. Decrease: $64k to $127k per month, depending on the baseline. $64k is the lowest figure.
False decline rate (share of good transactions declined): 2.46%, under the cap of 3%.

projects.title: Offer targeting for an email campaign
projects.result: $13k profit per campaign from an email to all customers, with no targeting model
projects.what: profit from an email to all customers, with no targeting model
projects.question: Which customers do we send the offer to, for the best return?
projects.answer: Send the men's email to all customers and keep a 10% holdout. It earns $13k per campaign of 100,000 customers.

keyline.p: Spend effect against the no-email group: +$0.77 per customer in the 2 weeks after the email.

keyline.h: The extra margin is larger than the contact cost
keyline.p: 30% margin on $0.77, less $0.10 for each email, gives $13,095 of profit per 100,000 customers. The email pays back at any cost below $0.23.

keyline.h: A targeting model adds nothing at this cost
keyline.p: Two uplift models did not beat a simple ranking by purchase history, and at $0.10 per email no segment earns more than an email to all customers.

uses: R
Runs the whole analysis in one notebook in base R.
Statistics
Designs and reads the experiment: power and sample size, Welch t-test, bootstrap, CUPED and the Holm correction.
Machine learning
Tests two uplift models (T-learner and uplift tree). They do not beat the ranking by purchase history, so the recommendation does not use them.
